lessons.title: Bacterial and viral diseases of slaughter stock
lessons.html:
Diseases the meat examiner must recognise

Meat inspection protects consumers from diseases that pass from animals to people (zoonoses), stops the spread of animal diseases, and removes meat that is unwholesome. Some diseases are controlled or notifiable under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984; suspected cases must be reported immediately to the responsible official and state veterinarian.

Important bacterial diseases

DiseaseSpeciesWhat to look for
Tuberculosis (TB)Cattle, pigs, othersYellowish, caseous (cheesy) or gritty calcified nodules in lymph nodes, lungs and other organs. Zoonotic.
AnthraxCattle, sheep, gameSudden death, dark unclotted blood from openings, enlarged spleen. Suspected carcasses must not be opened; report immediately. Zoonotic.
BrucellosisCattle, goats, pigsOften few carcass lesions; abortions on farm, inflamed testes, hygroma (swollen joints). Zoonotic.
Caseous lymphadenitisSheep, goatsAbscesses in lymph nodes with greenish, layered pus
Pneumonia (various bacteria)All speciesRed or grey, firm lung areas, pleuritis
SepticaemiaAll speciesGeneralised: haemorrhages, enlarged lymph nodes, poorly bled carcass

Viral diseases

  • Foot-and-mouth disease: blisters and erosions on mouth, tongue, feet and teats. Notifiable; report immediately.
  • Lumpy skin disease: nodules in skin and sometimes organs in cattle.
  • Rift Valley fever: liver damage, abortions; zoonotic and risky to people handling tissues.
  • African swine fever: haemorrhages in pigs; notifiable, devastating to the pig industry.
  • Rabies: nervous signs before slaughter; suspected animals must not be slaughtered for food.

When in doubt, detain the carcass and consult the meat inspector or veterinarian.

lessons.title: Parasitic diseases and other conditions
lessons.html:
Parasites in meat and organs

Cysticercosis (measles)

Measles are the cyst stage of human tapeworms. Beef measles (Cysticercus bovis) are the cysts of Taenia saginata; pork measles (Cysticercus cellulosae) are the cysts of Taenia solium, which is especially dangerous because people can also become infected with the cysts, including in the brain. Cysts appear as small, pale, fluid-filled bladders in muscles such as the heart, tongue, chewing muscles and diaphragm. Inspection includes prescribed incisions into these muscles. Depending on how many cysts are found, carcasses may be condemned or conditionally passed after treatment such as freezing, as the regulations specify.

Other parasites

  • Hydatid cysts (from dog tapeworm Echinococcus): large fluid-filled cysts in liver and lungs; condemn affected organs. Never feed offal to dogs.
  • Liver fluke: thickened bile ducts containing flat leaf-shaped flukes; liver condemned.
  • Sarcocystosis: small cysts in muscles; heavy infestations may cause condemnation.
  • Lungworms and nodular worms causing lesions in lungs and intestines.

Non-infectious conditions

ConditionNotes
BruisingTrim and condemn affected tissue
EmaciationWasting with gelatinous fat; often total condemnation
Jaundice (icterus)Yellow tissues; judgement depends on cause and degree
FracturesTrim surrounding tissue
TumoursSingle benign: condemn part; multiple or malignant spread: total condemnation
Abnormal odour (e.g. boar taint, medicinal smell)Detain for testing
ResiduesFrom remedies used without completing withdrawal periods; detected by sampling

Personal protection

Wear gloves and protective clothing, cover cuts, sterilise knives after cutting any lesion, wash hands, and do not eat in work areas. Report any work-related illness to your doctor and say that you work with animals and carcasses.

Key points

  • Report suspected notifiable diseases such as anthrax and foot-and-mouth immediately.
  • Never open a suspected anthrax carcass.
  • TB shows as cheesy or calcified nodules; measles as small fluid-filled cysts in muscles.
  • Pork measles (Taenia solium) can infect people with cysts.
  • Protect yourself from zoonoses with PPE, knife sterilising and hand washing.
